text:
In small, tightly knit herds of a dozen kin, the pebbleback auhk wallows in the Fenlands, chewing marsh plants and digging up mollusks 
to chew on their shells for the rich calcium they require to build up their namesake's bony plates. Th ough rather slow grazing beasts, 
predators keep a wary distance from them, for not only does their bony overlapping osteoderms give them a measure of protection from 
claw and tooth, their wide hardened horns can batter any would-be hunter into a muddy red ruin. While not particularly aggressive, 
there’s a certain obstinate movement in how they claim their wetland territories, sometimes even physically pushing baughur out of 
fertile swamps, relying on their armored hide to defend against any irritated, retaliatory tusked charges.

Encountering Wary of any that are not of their herd, the 
pebbleback auhk wade deeper into the marshes when an 
unknown creature approaches. If faced with aggression, three 
to four younger male bulls will charge forward dangerously in 
an effort to crush them. Th ough, even when frightened, the herd 
will not stampede for the marshes are plagued by sink holes that 
are quick to break the legs of even the hardiest of them. 
Wide and squat limbs wade through the 
Fenlands tirelessly, their four toed feet end 
in hoof-like nails that allow a strong grip in 
algae and mud-thick waters
Males sport a wide crest of horns, while 
the females themselves have a hardened 
forehead plate. Used to deter predators, 
the auhk can bludgeon and crush would- 
be predators with ease, protecting their 
young and feeding grounds
Rows of hardened osteoderms plates run 
down the back of auhk, giving rise to its 
namesake and protecting it while it wades 
in shallow waters eating marsh grass and 
shellfish. Little deters the large mammals 
from biting pests to aggressive predators
